paragraphs: Pollsters worry less about how many people decline to answer a survey than about whether those who decline differ from those who respond. A response rate of ten percent can yield an accurate portrait if refusals are scattered at random, while a rate of seventy percent can mislead if the missing thirty percent share a particular outlook. Researchers therefore compare their respondents with census figures on age, education and region and adjust the weights accordingly. The adjustment is helpful but cannot be a complete cure: it corrects only for the traits that were measured, and people who refuse to speak to strangers about politics may differ from their neighbors in ways that no census records. A modest degree of skepticism toward any single poll is therefore warranted.
